{{Short description|Data-driven algorithm}}
{{Orphan|date=June 2023}}

'''Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics''' ('''SINDy''') is a [[Data science|data-driven]] algorithm for obtaining [[dynamical system]]s from data.<ref>{{Cite book |author1-link=Steven L. Brunton |last1=Brunton |first1=Steven L. |last2=Kutz |first2=J. Nathan |date=2022-05-05 |title=Data-Driven Science and Engineering: Machine Learning, Dynamical Systems, and Control |url=https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/data-driven-science-and-engineering/6F9A730B7A9A9F43F68CF21A24BEC339 |access-date=2022-10-25 |publisher=Higher Education from Cambridge University Press |language=en |doi=10.1017/9781009089517|isbn=9781009089517 }}</ref> Given a series of [[Snapshot (computer storage)|snapshots]] of a dynamical system and its corresponding time [[derivative]]s, SINDy performs a [[Regularized least squares|sparsity-promoting]] regression (such as [[Lasso (statistics)|LASSO]] and sparse Bayesian inference<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Huang | first1 = Yunfei. | display-authors = etal | year = 2022 | title = Sparse inference and active learning of stochastic differential equations from data | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 12 | number = 1| article-number = 21691 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-022-25638-9  | pmid = 36522347 | doi-access = free| pmc = 9755218 | arxiv = 2203.11010 | bibcode = 2022NatSR..1221691H }}</ref>) on a library of [[Nonlinear system|nonlinear]] candidate [[Function (mathematics)|functions]] of the snapshots against the derivatives to find the governing [[equation]]s. This procedure relies on the assumption that most [[Physical system|physical]] systems only have a few dominant [[term (logic)|terms]] which dictate the dynamics, given an appropriately selected [[coordinate system]] and [[Data quality|quality training data]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brunton |first1=Steven L. |last2=Proctor |first2=Joshua L. |last3=Kutz |first3=J. Nathan |date=2016-04-12 |title=Discovering governing equations from data by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=113 |issue=15 |pages=3932–3937 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1517384113 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=4839439 |pmid=27035946|arxiv=1509.03580 |bibcode=2016PNAS..113.3932B |doi-access=free }}</ref> It has been applied to identify the dynamics of fluids, based on [[proper orthogonal decomposition]], as well as other complex dynamical systems, such as biological networks.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Mangan |first1=Niall M. |last2=Brunton |first2=Steven L. |last3=Proctor |first3=Joshua L. |last4=Kutz |first4=J. Nathan |date=2016-05-26 |title=Inferring biological networks by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics |class=math.DS |eprint=1605.08368}}</ref>

== Mathematical Overview ==
First, consider a dynamical system of the form

<math display="block">\dot{\textbf{x}}=\frac{d}{dt}\textbf{x}(t)=\textbf{f}(\textbf{x}(t)),</math>

where <math>\textbf{x}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n</math> is a state vector (snapshot) of the system at time <math>t</math> and the function <math>\textbf{f}(\textbf{x}(t))</math> defines the equations of motion and constraints of the system. The time derivative may be either prescribed or numerically approximated from the snapshots.

With <math>\textbf{x}</math> and <math>\dot{\textbf{x}}</math> sampled at <math>m</math> [[equidistant]] points in time (<math>t_1,t_2,\cdots,t_m</math>), these can be arranged into matrices of the form

<math display="block">\bf{X}=\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}(t_1) \\ \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}(t_2) \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}(t_m)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}x_1(t_1)&x_2(t_1)&\cdots&x_n(t_1)\\
x_1(t_2)&x_2(t_2)&\cdots&x_n(t_2)\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots \\
x_1(t_m)&x_2(t_m)&\cdots&x_n(t_m)
\end{bmatrix},</math>

and similarly for <math>\dot{\mathbf{X}}</math>.

Next, a library <math>\mathbf{\Theta}(\mathbf{X})</math> of nonlinear candidate functions of the columns of <math>\textbf{X}</math> is constructed, which may be constant, polynomial, or more exotic functions (like trigonometric and rational terms, and so on):

<math display="block">\ \ \ \bf{\Theta}(\bf{X})=\begin{bmatrix}
\vline&\vline&\vline&\vline& &\vline&\vline& \\
1&\bf{X}&\bf{X}^2&\bf{X}^3&\cdots & \sin(\bf{X})&\cos(\bf{X})&\cdots\\
\vline&\vline&\vline&\vline& &\vline&\vline&
\end{bmatrix}</math>

The number of possible model structures from this library is combinatorially high. <math>\textbf{f}(\textbf{x}(t))</math> is then substituted by <math>\bf{\Theta}(\textbf{X})</math> and a vector of coefficients <math>\bf{\Xi}=\left[\bf{\xi}_1 \bf{\xi}_2 \cdots \bf{\xi}_n \right]</math> determining the active terms in <math>\textbf{f}(\textbf{x}(t))</math>:

<math id="eq4" display="block">\dot{\bf{X}}=\bf{\Theta}(\bf{X})\bf{\Xi}</math>

Because only a few terms are expected to be active at each point in time, an assumption is made that <math>\textbf{f}(\textbf{x}(t))</math> admits a sparse representation in <math>\bf{\Theta}(\textbf{X})</math>. This then becomes an optimization problem in finding a sparse <math>\bf{\Xi}</math> which optimally embeds <math>\dot{\textbf{X}}</math>. In other words, a [[parsimonious]] model is obtained by performing least squares regression on the system {{EquationRef|(4)}} with sparsity-promoting (<math>L_1</math>) regularization

<math id="eq4" display="block">\bf{\xi}_k=\underset{\bf{\xi}'_k}{\arg\min}\left|\left|\dot{\bf{X}}_k-\bf{\Theta}(\bf{X})\bf{\xi}'_k\right|\right|_2 +\lambda \left|\left|\bf{\xi}'_k\right|\right|_1,</math>

where <math>\lambda</math> is a regularization parameter. Finally, the sparse set of <math>\bf{\xi}_k</math> can be used to reconstruct the dynamical system:

<math display="block">\dot{x}_k=\bf{\Theta}(\bf{x})\bf{\xi}_k</math>
